family.name: The act and what it hides
family.about: Fronts, personas and armour a character puts up so nobody sees the fear underneath.

entries.name: The I'm-fine front over a loss
entries.summary: A breezy, filthy, unbothered front that exists so the character never has to feel a loss, and that shows the loss every time it insists there isn't one.
entries.meaning: Picture the funniest person at the party who, you find out after they've gone, lost someone yesterday. The jokes aren't decoration on the sadness; they are how the person avoids feeling it, so when the front cracks, every earlier joke changes colour. The denial gives the feeling away: the more carefully someone insists they are fine, the plainer it is that they aren't, and the person having the grief never names it.
entries.in_pinder: The character believes the fun, filthy, unbothered version of them is the one worth matching, and that the sad version would end the chat on the spot. Their fear is that the loss is the real thing about them and that it shows. On the app they are relentlessly breezy: quick replies, big anecdotes, nothing with any weight. The reader sees the gap in small leaks the character steps over, like a detail too heavy for its sentence, an hour that makes no sense, or a joke that stops just short of a name. When something does land, they deny it and then explain the denial, each explanation more physical and elaborate than the last. It works best when the reader already knows what is being covered.

angles.author: Phoebe Waller-Bridge
angles.note: The front is competence, wit and sexual confidence held up over grief or guilt, and the drama is the moment it slips.

angles.author: Flight of the Conchords
angles.note: The denial escalates: each excuse for not being hurt is more detailed than the last, until the excuses are the confession.

origins.author: Phoebe Waller-Bridge

entries.name: Confidence covering panic
entries.summary: Total self-assurance about a big project, held up over someone who falls apart the moment anyone asks why.
entries.meaning: On the surface there is complete certainty: a grand project, a loud opinion, a man in charge. Underneath is someone one simple question from tears, and the question he dreads is 'why'. Both are visible at once, and the bigger the project, the more obviously it is holding something up.
entries.in_pinder: The character believes sounding certain is what gets you wanted, so they lead with big claims, plans and projects. What they fear is the plain question: why the outfit, why that photo, who it's for. They answer anything about the brag at length and anything about the reason in as few words as possible, then change the subject. The reader sees the boast and the tremor in the same few messages: a reply that suddenly goes short, a fast 'anyway'.

entries.name: Control as armour against rejection
entries.summary: A character who tries to plan every move of the conversation so nobody can surprise them with a no, and is thrown by an ordinary reply.
entries.meaning: Fielder goes in knowing what he will say and where the scene should go, and real people send it somewhere he couldn't predict. The persona believes enough foresight will make other people safe, and the work keeps showing that it doesn't. Read as a character, he is a lonely man who builds full-scale replicas of social situations because he can't bear not knowing how a conversation will go.
entries.in_pinder: The character believes rejection is a failure of planning: anticipate every move and nobody can surprise you with a no. Their fear is the reply they didn't see coming, because that is where they can be hurt. On the app they predict the other's answers, answer objections nobody has raised, offer contingencies, and are knocked flat by a perfectly normal message. The reader sees that every precaution is aimed at a rejection the precautions themselves are bringing on.

entries.name: Flatness as armour
entries.summary: A character who says everything at the same level so nobody can see where to hit, which makes the one break in tone the biggest event in the chat.

entries.name: Rehearsing life so it goes well
entries.summary: A character who has prepared their lines in advance and steers the chat back to the script, which shows more of them than anything unplanned would.

entries.name: Saving face at ruinous cost
entries.summary: Caught in a tiny mistake, the character refuses to admit it, and the cover-up costs far more than the mistake ever could.
entries.meaning: A small social slip that would cost nothing to admit becomes a disaster because the person cannot bear to be seen getting it wrong. The writers' principle behind this work is that nothing is funnier than someone embarrassed, because to save face they dig a deeper hole and reveal something worse than the original offence. Blaming something else is treated as an instinct, a little self-protection, not a plan. The offence is tiny; the cover-up is enormous.
entries.in_pinder: The character believes that being seen wrong about one small thing is fatal: the match will notice and leave. What they fear is that single visible moment of error, whether it's a bad angle, a misread compliment or a number in the bio. Caught out, they never say 'fair'; they build a structure around the mistake, and every message makes the structure bigger and gives away something new. The reader sees a slip that would cost nothing to own and watches the character pay everything not to.

origins.author: Tim Robinson
origins.text: The report says saving face after a small humiliation, at ruinous cost, runs through all his work, from the hot-dog-costume man to the Titanic-replica billionaire to Ron's fall from a chair.

entries.name: Cruelty in a sweet voice
entries.summary: A compliment that lands exactly on the other person's sore spot.
entries.how_it_works: The words are warm and the effect is a blade. The reader hears the compliment and the damage at once, and the gap between them is chilling and darkly funny. Because it's sweet, the target can't easily fight back.
entries.in_pinder: Use it at the collision or the collapse: one character's defence comes out as praise that hits precisely where the other is sore, which the reader knows and the speaker may not. Put it in its own short message after something vulnerable. The speaker should mean it kindly, or believe they do.
entries.test: Read the line alone: is it a compliment, and does it land on the exact fear the reader knows the other has?
entries.goes_wrong: If the speaker knows it's cruel and enjoys it, they become the villain the brief forbids. If it isn't tied to an established sore spot, it's just nasty.

entries.name: A swerve in tone instead of a punchline
entries.summary: A bright message drops into something bleak and carries on brightly, as if nothing happened.
entries.how_it_works: There is no constructed joke; the laugh comes from the temperature dropping without warning and the crack showing in the surface. It works because the character doesn't register the drop, so the reader is the only one who sees it.
entries.in_pinder: Put the swerve inside one message, or across back-to-back messages from the same character: cheerful, then a bleak detail, then cheerful again. The bleak detail should be specific and say something about the fear. It is most useful in the act and early middle, where it hints at the why before it is revealed, and it changes temperature within a single turn.

entries.name: Describe yourself as an object
entries.summary: A character states, flatly, that they are a specific household object, and the comparison gives them away.
entries.how_it_works: Saying you are a thing compresses a whole personality into one image the reader can picture and judge. It shows a feeling as a picture instead of having the character explain it.
entries.in_pinder: Give a character one comparison to a specific domestic object, in their bio or early chat, stated as fact. entries.name: An exact odd image instead of a punchline
entries.summary: One precise, slightly wrong picture from the character's life, stated plainly, does the work a punchline would.
entries.how_it_works: A precise picture makes the reader do the seeing, and the laugh comes when it snaps into focus. There is no joke-shaped sentence to brace against, so it reads as a true report rather than a bit. The oddness of the detail also tells you about the person who noticed it.
entries.in_pinder: Put the image in one plain message with no setup saying it's funny. Zoom in to one object, one position, one sound, rather than a whole scene. It works best in the act, when the reader is learning what this dick's world looks like, and in the middle when a detail of their flat or body slips out. Make the filth this exact too: not 'I'm kinky' but the exact thing on the bedside table.

entries.goes_wrong: The detail turns into a list of quirky items, or gets a follow-up explaining why it's funny. Whimsy that isn't attached to something embarrassing goes precious.

entries.name: Specific self-deprecation, never general
entries.summary: Instead of 'I'm a mess', the character tells one exact humiliating incident, worst detail last.

entries.name: Notice the wrong thing
entries.summary: A character tells a painful story and fixes on a trivial detail inside it, so the reader sees the wound he doesn't mention.
entries.how_it_works: The speaker reports a disaster but gives his attention to a small detail inside it. The reader sees the disaster clearly because he doesn't. The laugh is the gap between where the character is looking and where the reader is.
entries.in_pinder: A character tells how he was ghosted, dumped by text or left at the restaurant, and lingers on the font, the dessert, the tip. The reader sees the wound he never names. entries.goes_wrong: The character names the wound too ('anyway that hurt'), or the trivial detail is so loud that the wound is invisible to the reader as well.

entries.name: Impossible premise, practical consequence
entries.summary: Something impossible about the character is stated as fact, and what worries them is its dull practical fallout.
entries.how_it_works: The reader accepts the premise because the speaker clearly does, and the laugh comes from the consequence: sober, logistical, worried about exactly the wrong thing. The bigger the premise and the smaller the consequence, the harder the laugh.
entries.in_pinder: A character states something absurd about his body, flat or past in one message, and deals with its practical fallout in the next. The premise must come from the character's injury, not random invention: his absurd fact is the shape of his fear. It works best in the act, to establish how he copes, and in the middle as a doubled-down explanation when he's caught.
entries.test: Is the consequence smaller and more practical than the premise, and does the character seem more worried about the consequence?
entries.goes_wrong: The premise is random surrealism with no link to who the character is, a portable one-liner that gives nothing away. Or the character signals it's a bit.

entries.name: Grand claim, then a small exact comparison
entries.summary: A big claim about the character's flat, body or life, followed by a precise comparison they think is a selling point and which deflates it.
entries.how_it_works: The reader builds a big picture, and one precise small detail lets the air out. The precision is what makes it land: a vague undercut is just modesty, while an exact one shows how the speaker really sees their world.
entries.in_pinder: In stand-up the undercut is self-aware; in Pinder the character must mean the comparison as a boast and not notice that it deflates. Put the grand claim in one message and the exact comparison in the next, so the break is the pause. It fits the act best: their flat, their body, their weekend. The comparison should come from their own life, so it gives them away.

entries.goes_wrong: The character knows it's a letdown and plays it for laughs, which is a wink. Or the comparison is generic ('it's tiny lol') and reveals nothing.

entries.name: The mundane undercut after a big build
entries.summary: A message builds to an emergency and the next one reveals something small, ordinary and domestic.
entries.how_it_works: The build tells the reader to expect something enormous, and the payoff is small and ordinary. Use the deflating version for pace and the reverse version to show a character who can't let big things in.

entries.goes_wrong: The undercut comes with a self-aware tag ('lol anticlimax'), or the build is half-hearted so there is nowhere to fall from.

entries.name: Cut to the fewest words
entries.summary: Cut each message to the fewest words that still land, plus one for rhythm, and strip the line that matters most down to the bare fact.
entries.how_it_works: Every extra word gives the reader time to see the turn coming or drift away, so cutting makes the turn hit as a surprise. A bare fact feels true, and the absence of explanation lets the reader supply the emotion. But a line with no rhythm lands flat, so one non-essential word can stay if it makes the line sound spoken. Adding lines to a joke that isn't working makes it worse.
entries.in_pinder: Cut each message until it breaks, then put back the one word that makes it sound like this character texting; tics and fillers ('anyway', 'honestly', 'I mean') are usually that word. It matters most for punchline messages and for the plain tender line, which should be the shortest in the chat: no adjectives, no feelings named, no hedges, set after longer messages so its shortness is an event. Stop before it becomes a riddle: the reader has to decode it from what's already on the screen.
entries.test: Cut each word in turn: does the line still land? If yes, cut it, unless the line then stops sounding like this character or can no longer be decoded from earlier messages.
entries.goes_wrong: Messages trimmed so far they lose the character's voice and read like telegrams from the writer, or compressed into a riddle only the writer understands. Or a punchline or plain line padded with an explanation of the feeling.

entries.name: A dating rule recited as law
entries.summary: A character states a precise, made-up dating rule as common etiquette and applies it mechanically where it doesn't fit.
entries.how_it_works: The rule is absurdly precise and stated as something everyone knows, so the reader recognises both the rule and the kind of person who lives by it. The laugh comes when it is applied mechanically to a situation it doesn't fit, by someone who believes in it completely.
entries.in_pinder: The character states a rule as obvious etiquette, and the screen already shows it being broken or producing something ridiculous. Each challenge gets a more elaborate application of the rule, never a retreat. Invent the character's own rule and let it grow out of their fear: a rule about reply times belongs to someone afraid of looking keen. No citing studies or figures; it's simply something they know.
entries.test: Is the rule stated as plain fact, and does the screen already show it being broken or bent?
entries.goes_wrong: The character cites research or numbers, which is the day-job voice the brief bans, or drops the rule the first time it's challenged.

entries.name: Taking dating phrases literally
entries.summary: A character takes an app slogan or body word at face value and follows the literal meaning, with total confidence, in the direction their fear wants.
entries.how_it_works: Everyone knows the figurative meaning of the phrase; the speaker commits to the literal one and follows it to its conclusion without flagging the misreading, so it sounds like logic rather than a pun. The laugh is the collision of the two meanings, plus recognition: we've all said the phrase and never heard what it says. A shirt that says dry clean only is, therefore, dirty.
entries.in_pinder: Aim it at the phrases the app and dating culture hand out ('high value', 'no strings', 'emotionally available', 'out of my league', 'let's see where it goes') and at body words (thick, hung, grower, cut). The label can sit in the other person's message or a quoted bio with the literal reading in the reply, or the character can say it of themselves and live by it over several messages. The misreading should serve the character's fear, so it gives them away and shows how empty the slogan was. It can come back later as a callback when the literal meaning turns out to be true.
entries.test: Could a reader underline the one dating phrase the exchange is built on, and does the literal reading serve the character's own defence rather than just being a play on words?
entries.goes_wrong: It turns into a pun the character seems pleased with, which is winking. Or the misreading is portable: it has no fear behind it and says nothing about who made it.

angles.note: The misreading is a single confident step: someone else's label, taken at its word, delivered as a conclusion.

entries.summary: A self-care slogan recited as wisdom turns out, a message later, to be a sulk, a dodge or a dig at the match.

entries.in_pinder: The character recites a dating-culture slogan ('that's information about them', 'I'm protecting my peace', 'what's meant for me will come') as if it were wisdom, and the next message shows what it is for. Put the slogan and its real use in separate messages so the reader catches the turn. It works best under pressure, when the character is kept waiting or turned down, and it gives the satire a voice without a speech. When caught, the character defends the slogan rather than dropping it.

entries.goes_wrong: The character says it knowingly, as an ironic quote, or the slogan is generic and could belong to anyone instead of showing this person's particular sore spot.

entries.name: Therapy-speak used as a weapon
entries.summary: A character wraps a jab, accusation or excuse in soft therapy forms and believes the wrapping makes it fair.
entries.how_it_works: The form is soft and careful while the content is an attack or an alibi. The softer the packaging, the more naked the aggression inside looks. Because the speaker believes the format makes the attack fair, they never notice the distance, and the reader can't stop noticing it.
entries.in_pinder: The character, never the writer, uses therapy and wellness forms: I statements, 'holding space', boundaries, 'I hear you'. Each message is wrapped in that form and carries a jab, an accusation or an excuse, and the screen contradicts the calm it claims. It is strongest in the middle, when the two acts collide and one character fights without admitting they are fighting. Keep the vocabulary to what dating culture really says, and keep it the character's armour, never the narration.
entries.test: Strip out the therapy wording: is what remains an attack or an excuse? If nothing hostile or self-serving is left, it's just therapy-speak, so cut it.
entries.goes_wrong: The writer's own voice turns therapeutic and characters start sincerely explaining their feelings, which the brief bans; or the form has no hidden content, so there is no gap.

entries.name: Airtight inside logic, absurd result
entries.summary: A character reasons one sensible step at a time, inside dating logic or their own private rules, to an insane conclusion.
entries.how_it_works: Each justification is sound on its own terms, so the reader can't find the step where it went wrong, and the laugh is the distance between sensible reasoning and an absurd result. The chain has to be airtight: one hole and the character is merely random instead of unhinged.
entries.in_pinder: Give the character one framework, from dating culture or from their own rules about their body, sex or exes, and let them reason with it one plausible message at a time. Each message should be defensible read alone; the absurdity only shows across the run. Put the conclusion in its own message so it lands after the reasoning. The logic must be dating-app logic or the character's own, never workplace or spreadsheet talk.

entries.goes_wrong: A non sequitur in the chain makes the character random instead of unhinged; corporate or data vocabulary breaks the brief's rule against talking like a day job.

entries.name: Each excuse worse than the last
entries.summary: Caught out, the character offers one excuse after another, each adding a new and worse fact, until the last and plainest one is a confession they pass over as more cover.
entries.how_it_works: Each attempt to close the question introduces a new fact, and the new fact is worse than the thing it was meant to excuse. The reader can see the character could stop at any point and won't, and the effort going into the cover story measures the feeling behind it. The order is the craft: the reveals have to climb, and the one that hurts most is a small, plain detail that slips in disguised as just another excuse.
entries.in_pinder: One excuse per message, so the message breaks are the steps down the hole. Each excuse should follow the character's own logic and be a fresh, more physical cause. The last message holds the confession: shorter and plainer than the rest, offered as cover, and the character moves straight on. Nothing follows it, and the other character does not point out what was just confessed. This is the cleanest way for a piece of the why to get out in the middle of a chat without anyone explaining anything.
entries.test: Does each message add one new fact that is worse than the one before, and is the most revealing line also the shortest and plainest, passed over as if it were more cover?
entries.goes_wrong: The excuses are random instead of following the character's logic; the run keeps going after the confession and lets the air out; the confession arrives as a long, articulate message; or the character or the other person recognises it and comments on it.

angles.author: Tim Robinson

angles.author: Flight of the Conchords
angles.note: The last excuse is a sad, plain fact dressed as one more excuse, so the denial makes the grief obvious and the plainness makes it hurt.

angles.author: Sharon Horgan

entries.name: The correction that makes it worse
entries.summary: The character corrects a claim about themselves, and each correction lands further in, offered in earnest as an improvement.
entries.how_it_works: A correction promises relief: the reader expects the claim to be walked back or repaired. Instead it moves further in or swings to something more damning, so the expected rescue is reversed and the admission ends larger than it began. In trying to look better, the character reveals more than the original claim hid.
entries.in_pinder: Three or four messages: the claim, the correction in its own message, and a correction of the correction or a justification that digs deeper. Each message break is a beat where the reader expects things to get better. It fits any claim a character makes about themselves: length, count, time since the ex. entries.goes_wrong: The corrections wander sideways instead of deeper; the character laughs at their own correction; or they end with a concession ('ok fine I'm a mess'), which collapses the double-down into a wink.

entries.name: Blame a nearby object
entries.summary: Caught out, the character's first move is to pin it on something specific in their surroundings, and the thing they blame gives them away.
entries.how_it_works: Deflecting onto something inanimate is a reflex everyone recognises, so the reader laughs at self-protection that is both obvious and small; objects can't answer back, which makes the excuse safe for the character and absurd to everyone else. When the blamed thing is oddly specific and said sincerely, the explanation turns out weirder and more revealing than what it explains.
entries.in_pinder: Straight after the catch, the character's reply names one specific thing: the cold flat, the jeans, the cheap ring light, the bathroom mirror, the heart animation. Pinder's bodies make it rich: shrinkage, curve, angle and colour all have a thing to blame. Keep it to a message or two as the opening move of a doubling-down run, not the whole run. The thing blamed should be specific to this person's life and, said as an ordinary explanation, should accidentally show the fear underneath; often it carries the first piece of the why.
entries.test: Is the reply one named object or condition specific to this character, more revealing than the behaviour it explains, and said with no awareness of that?
entries.goes_wrong: The object is generic ('bad lighting lol') and reads like a quip that fills a turn; the character is enjoying a clever excuse, which is sly instead of sincere; the redirect reveals nothing about them; or nothing follows it and the deflection simply goes nowhere.

entries.name: The persona cracks, then gets patched worse

entries.name: Escalate in small reasonable steps
entries.summary: A request or plan climbs one individually reasonable notch at a time until it is alarming, each step defended by the one before.
entries.how_it_works: No single step is a leap, so the reader is carried along and only sees how far they have come when they look back. Each increment is justified by the previous one. The ladder has to stay tied to something believable, or it turns cartoonish.
entries.in_pinder: One notch per message or per exchange, each a reasonable response to what came before, including the other's reply. The other's pushback should be what moves the next step up, not what stops it. Most useful in the middle, where the two acts collide. entries.goes_wrong: Skipped rungs make it random; with no ceiling the character becomes a cartoon and the need underneath disappears.

entries.name: Punchline in the next message
entries.summary: Put a plain, believable setup in one message and the line that turns it in the next, so the send button does the job of the pause.
entries.how_it_works: The first line sounds reasonable, and the pause lets the reader accept it and build an expectation. The next line keeps the same footing but turns it inside out or sideways, so the reader has to reread the first line after already believing it. The break between bubbles is the pause, and the rewriting of something already believed is the laugh.
entries.in_pinder: Setup in one message, turn in the next, never bundled. The turn can open with "because", simply arrive as the next fact, or reveal that a word in the setup meant something else. It can be split across speakers: one character's innocent message is the setup and the other's reply turns it, and a one-word reaction between the two makes the turn land harder. It works from the opener to the collapse, but not every turn, or the rhythm becomes a machine.
entries.test: Read the first message alone: does it sound perfectly ordinary and reasonable? It should, and only the next message should turn it.
entries.goes_wrong: The turn is folded into the setup's bubble so the pause is lost; the second line merely explains the first instead of turning it; or a third message explains the turn.

entries.name: One-word reply as a reaction shot
entries.summary: After a long or unhinged run, the other character answers with one word, which shows who is in trouble and makes them keep typing.
entries.how_it_works: Watching someone receive the absurd thing lets the reader feel it, and a blank reaction refuses to do the laughing for them, so they do it themselves. The reaction also moves the tension onto the person making the scene, so a doubling-down run reads as their trouble rather than as the writer bullying them. And a short reply after a long message is a held silence: the writer of the long one has to fill it, and filling it is where they give themselves away.
entries.in_pinder: After one character's run or long message, the other replies with one word or a fragment as its own message: 'ok', 'right', '?', '...', or an echo of the worst detail ('the bath?'). Put it straight after the worst line, at the peak of the run. The first character then keeps typing into it, and each message digs deeper. Use it once or twice a chat; a real silence, shown by a '…' or by a next line that is clearly much later, is an event to spend once, after the most revealing message.
entries.test: Is the reply shorter than every message in the run before it, does it come right after the worst line, and is the next message from the person who now has to fill the gap?
entries.goes_wrong: The reply is a mocking quip ('wow lol'), which makes the reactor the comedian and the other a victim and does the reader's job; or it is used so often that the reactor becomes a wall with no act of their own and the chat reads as dying; or it is a cold put-down with no fear behind it.

angles.author: Tim Robinson
angles.note: The reaction is what keeps a doubling-down run from feeling cruel, and echoing the worst detail back is the sharpest version.

entries.name: Cut the message at the gap

entries.name: The silence as a message
entries.summary: A gap in replies is a beat in itself, shown only by what the next messages say, and the one who waited fills it with the worst reading.
entries.how_it_works: Texting trains people to expect an answer at once, so an absence becomes a statement and the one waiting pours meaning into it, usually anger or rejection. The laugh, or the wince, is how much someone makes of nothing.

entries.name: Let a piece of the reason slip
entries.summary: When the why comes out, give one concrete fact in passing, never the whole cause, and let the reader assemble the rest.
entries.how_it_works: A single tidy cause closes a character: once the audience has the explanation, the behaviour becomes a symptom and stops surprising them. One fragment, an outcome plus a precise detail, keeps them a person, because the reader can feel there is more and their imagination fills the gap with something worse and funnier than any telling. Said offhand, as if the character finds it ordinary, the fragment reframes the habit as protection, so the earlier laughs change temperature without stopping.
entries.in_pinder: Give one concrete fragment: an object, a parent's habit, a single event, not a diagnosis and no feeling named. It arrives sideways in one or two plain messages, often as the answer to a plain question from the match or as a clause in a message about something else, and then the character goes straight back to the act. If the match asks for more, the answer gets shorter, not longer. It works best in the middle, after the reader has laughed at the habit; a bare clause can also be planted early and only understood later.
entries.test: Is the reveal a fact rather than a feeling, shorter than the message before it, and could the reader still ask 'but why that?' afterwards? If it explains everything, cut it down.
entries.goes_wrong: The character summarises their own psychology ('I think because my dad left I...'), tells the whole story when asked, or the reveal comes before the habit has been laughed at; each does the reader's work for them.

When the script shows, the audience sees the performance and the frightened person who wrote it at the same time. The sender then has to defend it, and the defence is where the laugh lives, because it reveals what they were afraid of.
entries.in_pinder: Open with a line the reader can tell has gone to forty people, or let the rehearsal leak as a medium disaster: a template pasted with the wrong name or hobby, an answer to the question they prepared for instead of the one asked, or the match catching it ('you sent me this on monday'). It happens to the character once. They don't concede; they explain or defend it as strategy, and the explanation gives away more than the slip, usually a fear of being turned down if they try properly. A line prepared early can also come back word for word later, where it fits too well or too badly. This is the brief's satire directly: the app rewards the opener you've sent to everyone.
entries.test: Does the leaked or defended line tell the reader something about the character's fear that they haven't said, and is it generic enough to mass-send but specific enough that only this character would send it?
entries.goes_wrong: The sender laughs it off or apologises at once ('lol copy paste fail'), which is a concession and a wink together; the opener is a stock pickup line with no person in it; or the leak happens twice and becomes a gimmick.

entries.name: The commentary meant for someone else
entries.summary: Give the character a private audience off the chat and let one message of commentary meant for them land in the match's window.
entries.how_it_works: A running private commentary for someone who will get the joke shows the gap between what a person says to people and what they really think. On Pinder it can't go to the reader without a wink, but it can go to someone inside the story. When it lands in the wrong window, the private commentary and the public act are on the same screen at once.
entries.in_pinder: Give the character a witness: a group chat, a sibling, a parent, a friend who never replies. Let the commentary misfire into the match's window once: the misdirected message, then the correction, then an explanation that makes it worse. Who the witness is should be revealing in itself, ideally connected to what the character lost or fears. Once per chat; a second misfire reads as a device.
entries.test: Is the misdirected message written for its intended recipient, in a voice the match was never meant to see, and does it change how the earlier messages read?
entries.goes_wrong: The commentary is addressed to no one in particular and reads as the writer nudging the reader, or the misfire is cute and changes nothing.

entries.name: Getting caught performing
entries.summary: The match names the act plainly, using evidence already on the screen, and the character either digs deeper or answers in one word.
entries.how_it_works: The act worked as long as nobody saw it. When the one person paying attention finally does, the device becomes the plot and the floor goes. The laugh is the shock of the private thing said out loud, plainly, by someone who isn't playing along.
entries.in_pinder: Let the match name the act in one or two plain messages, citing what the reader has already seen: reply times, the same line twice, the story that doesn't add up. The character has two moves: double down with a worse explanation, or answer in one word. The one-word answer is often the chat's turning point. Make the danger visible a turn early so the reader sees the catch coming before the character does.
entries.test: Does the catch rely only on things already on the screen, and is the answer either bigger or one word, never a measured concession?
entries.goes_wrong: The match diagnoses the character in therapy-speak ('I think you use humour to deflect'), or the character concedes gracefully at the first hit.

entries.name: The late reveal that recolours everything
entries.summary: Hold back the reason for a habit until it has been laughed at several times, so its arrival makes the reader reread every earlier line.
entries.how_it_works: Early on, the habit plays as comedy and the reader judges the character a little for it. When the withheld fact arrives, every earlier joke turns out to have been about it, so the reader laughs again in retrospect, differently, and judgement turns into affection. The jokes don't change; the reader's reading of them does, and the pleasure is doing that reinterpretation themselves.
entries.in_pinder: Decide early what the character is withholding and plant it in incidental details during the act, so the opening jokes are compatible with it without pointing at it. Establish the habit several times as just a funny thing they do. Let the fact out in the middle or late, sideways and briefly: a slip, a throwaway, a message meant for someone else, rarely a deliberate confession. Two or three short lines usually beat one long message, though a long message is an event and can carry it once. Afterwards, bring the habit back once without comment so the reader feels the difference.
entries.test: After the reveal, reread the first third: do at least two earlier lines change meaning without a word of them changing and without anyone pointing at them?
entries.goes_wrong: The reveal is a tidy trauma explanation that accounts for everything, it arrives too early to reframe anything, or a character spells out the connection ('I guess that's why I do it').

angles.author: Phoebe Waller-Bridge
angles.note: Builds the whole act on top of the withheld fact, so the filthiest, breeziest jokes turn out to have been about the worst thing.

angles.author: Jenny Slate
angles.note: After the reveal, returns to the habit once, unchanged, so the reader feels it land sad or sweet.

entries.name: The throwaway that turns out huge
entries.summary: Plant a detail so small and incidental the reader files it as texture, then let it come back carrying the weight of the chat.
entries.how_it_works: A detail planted as noise is too small to be suspicious, so the reader skims past it. When it returns carrying weight, they realise it was the most important thing all along, and the laugh or gasp is them putting it together. The smaller the first mention, the bigger the turn.
entries.in_pinder: Plant something incidental early, inside a message about something else: an object, a habit, a person mentioned in passing. Let it come back once in the middle, still looking like a throwaway. At the payoff, a single line uses it so that it means something else, and nobody explains it. The best plants are filthy or silly on first appearance, because that is where they hide.
entries.test: On first appearance, would a reader skim past it? At the payoff, is it left unexplained?
entries.goes_wrong: The plant is flagged so heavily the reader sees it coming, or a character explains the callback at the payoff.

entries.name: The known line with one new clause
entries.summary: Bring an early line back nearly word for word, then add one clause that changes what it meant all along.
entries.how_it_works: The payoff relies on the reader already knowing the original: they recognise the line, expect the familiar ending, and one added clause bends it into something new. The laugh is recognition and surprise at once.
entries.in_pinder: Plant a line early as a throwaway habit or rule. Bring it back near the end nearly word for word, then put the single added clause in its own next message so the break does the timing. Nobody comments on it. The repeat must be close enough that the reader spots the echo without being told.
entries.test: Is the returning line nearly word for word, with exactly one added clause, and does nobody explain what it now means?
entries.goes_wrong: The callback is paraphrased so loosely the echo is lost, or someone explains it.

entries.name: The insecure check-in, repeated

entries.how_it_works: Asking for reassurance once is human; asking too often turns the need into a visible tic, and the reader laughs at a hunger they recognise. Because it repeats, the reader starts anticipating it, which turns it into a setup.
entries.in_pinder: Give the character a check-in in their own wording and repeat it at the worst moments: right after something good, mid-flirt, one message in. Space it so the reader starts counting. Then reverse it: late in the chat the other one asks it plainly, and the habitual asker answers in a word, a status flip nobody explains.

entries.name: The callback that lands hardest last

entries.in_pinder: Plant an odd small detail in the first third, bring it back once in the middle so it stays alive, and return to it in the ending in a shorter form with a changed meaning. Nobody explains the return; the line is short and plain. The details most worth calling back are the character's own image for their body or a very exact object.

entries.goes_wrong: The callback is announced ('like what you said earlier about…') or comes back so often it becomes a catchphrase.

entries.name: A running word, never explained
entries.summary: Give the character one odd, precise phrase for something and let it recur verbatim, never defined.
entries.how_it_works: An odd, specific word used again becomes the character's private vocabulary. The reader starts waiting for it, and because it's never explained they fill it in themselves, which is more fun than being told.
entries.in_pinder: Give the character one odd, precise phrase for their erection, their ex or their flat, and let it come back three or four times across the chat, verbatim and never defined. It doesn't have to flip meaning; it just builds. Bring it back only when it fits the moment, not because it worked last time.
entries.test: Is it one specific phrase, used verbatim each time, and does nobody ever explain it?
entries.goes_wrong: The match asks what it means and gets an answer, or it shows up every turn until it's wallpaper.

entries.name: Shorter each time it comes back
entries.summary: Each time a habit recurs, cut it shorter, until a single word lands at exactly the wrong moment.
entries.how_it_works: Once the reader knows the shape, a long setup lets them finish it first and the laugh dies. Shortening each version gets the turn in before they can, and the brevity becomes its own laugh of recognition.
entries.in_pinder: Give the habit in full first, then half, then a word or two. By the third time the reader is primed, so the short version lands, and it can be aimed at exactly the wrong moment for a wince. A short return answering a long or warm message also gives the temperature change the brief asks for.
entries.test: Is each recurrence shorter than the last, and has the reader seen the full version before the shortest one?
entries.goes_wrong: The habit returns at full length every time and the reader gets ahead of it, or it's cut to one word before the reader has learned it, so it means nothing.

entries.how_it_works: A fact that would be a good joke early is worth more late, when the reader can see everything it explains. Withholding it lets the setup sit unexplained, so when it arrives it connects everything at once and the reader does the connecting.

entries.in_pinder: Let one character build a theory about why the other went cold, every part of it about their own body or messages. Then let the other's reason come out plainly, as a piece of their own history, so it deflates the spiral and shows the reader where the second one's habit comes from. Nobody points out the mismatch.

entries.name: Misread threat, deflated by their shame
entries.summary: An ambiguous message makes a character think they've been found out, they half-confess, and the other's real news is a small shame of their own.

entries.in_pinder: It only works if the character's secret is already on screen or obvious from their act. The other sends something ambiguous ('I have to tell you something before we meet'), the character confesses in a panic, and the other's real confession turns out small, specific and about themselves. It gives a wince and a status flip, and both characters some madness.

entries.goes_wrong: The secret wasn't set up, so the over-reaction reads as random, or the other's confession is a quip instead of a real, specific small shame.

family.name: Plain and tender lines
family.about: How closeness shows up through short, plain, practical or gross-but-loving lines rather than declarations.

entries.name: Plainness at the peak
entries.summary: At the most naked moment, the character sends the shortest, plainest message in the chat, and nobody explains it.
entries.how_it_works: After a long run of fast, ornate or filthy talk, a short plain line has nothing to hide behind, so it reads as the truth. The reader has learned how much this character talks to avoid saying things, so the line with almost nothing in it is the loudest one in the chat. Braced for big emotion, the reader gets a plain fact and adds the weight themselves, and what is missing from the line is part of what it says.
entries.in_pinder: Give the character the shortest, plainest message they have sent: a few words, no joke, no filth, often lower-case and unpunctuated. Put it after a long message from the other side so it also works as a reaction shot. The reply should be just as short, and nobody names the feeling. A long message is allowed only when it is a plain account of what happened, not of how it felt. Don't follow the line with an explanation, and save it for the why or the ending.
entries.test: Is this the shortest and plainest line the character has sent, with no feeling named, and does it stand without a follow-up explaining it?
entries.goes_wrong: The character follows the plain line by explaining what it meant or what it did to them, which is therapy-speak; the line uses feeling words instead of a small concrete thing; or the other character answers with paragraphs of comfort and does the reader's work.

entries.name: Loss as a small plain fact
entries.summary: A loss is stated as one small, flat piece of information, in the character's usual voice, with no word for the feeling.
entries.how_it_works: Grief stated without adjectives or self-pity leaves the reader to supply the feeling, and they supply more than the speaker could. The small, flat statement against the size of the loss creates the ache, and it can stay funny because the speaker treats it as just information. If the voice doesn't change, the sadness arrives without warning and the reader realises the jokes came from the same place.
entries.in_pinder: Give the loss one short message, the shortest in its run, with no emotional vocabulary. Put it after a longer or sillier message so the temperature drops sharply. Ideally it comes out of the character's established habit: the thing they always notice or list, except this time the detail is from their childhood or their loneliness, with no change of tone and no announcement. The other character doesn't console at length; a short reply or a change of subject keeps it raw. Used for the why, it makes the reader reread the earlier jokes.

entries.how_it_works: A declaration asks the reader to take the speaker's word; an automatic gesture proves it, because the person didn't think to make a point of it. The offhandedness is what makes it hit. Making the tender line an action rather than a feeling word keeps it understated, so the reader hears the love in what is offered, not in what is said.
entries.in_pinder: Near the end, one character mentions a small kindness they would do or already did for the other, as a practical detail: a towel, a hot water bottle, which side of the bed. It is shorter than the messages around it and nothing explains it; the reply is short too, or a silence. One strong shape: a long, specific complaint about everything that could go wrong with the match, the flat or their bodies, then, in its own message, one short concrete offer that solves one of those problems. It can be filthy, as long as the care is in a practical detail rather than a speech.

entries.name: The true gross thing, taken as love
entries.summary: Where a normal person would be polite, the character says the true, specific, slightly disgusting thing about their body, and the other takes it as love.
entries.how_it_works: The reader expects the social script (a compliment, a white lie, discretion) and gets the unfiltered truth instead; the surprise gets the laugh. The other person not flinching, or answering with relief or a confession of their own, turns the laugh warm, because the reader knows what the confession cost. Acceptance is shown, never said.
entries.in_pinder: Put the polite expectation in one message and the honest, specific, physical truth in the next. Use it late, once both acts and both shames are established and one character is starting to drop the act: the gross truth is the first real thing they've said, delivered as plain information, not as a bit. The strongest reply is not reassurance but enthusiasm, recognition or a matching, more specific flaw of the other's own. This is where bravado turns into intimacy.
entries.test: Does the line replace a polite thing with something true and specific to this body, and does the reply match it with a specific rather than reassure?
entries.goes_wrong: The character knows it's shocking and enjoys it, which is winking edginess; the filth is generic and gives nothing away; the other reassures ('honestly don't worry about it'), which is therapy; or it comes before the shame is established and is only a gross-out.

entries.name: Accurate insult as proof of attention
entries.summary: One character insults the other with a precise detail from earlier in the chat, and the accuracy shows they've been watching.
entries.how_it_works: A generic insult is aggression; a precise one is intimacy, because it could only come from someone who noticed. The laugh is the accuracy, and the warmth is realising the insulter has been paying close attention. The receiver's pleasure at being seen sells it.
entries.in_pinder: Use it as a sign of connection from the middle on, once there's enough on the screen to be accurate about. The insult uses a detail from much earlier (a photo, a typo, a claim in the bio), so it doubles as a callback. The receiver answers with a short concession or a precise insult back, not with hurt.
entries.test: Could this insult only be said to this person, using something already on the screen?
entries.goes_wrong: The insult is generic or about something the reader hasn't seen, so it's just a quip; or it lands on the real sore spot without warmth and becomes cruel.

entries.name: Undercut the tender moment, leave it standing
entries.summary: A plain tender line is followed by a crude, specific one that punctures it without taking it back.
entries.how_it_works: The tender line lands, and before it can go soft the next line punctures it with something crude, but the crude line shows the feeling was real. The undercut keeps the reader from sentimentality and keeps the characters in character. Done well, the joke makes the tenderness more believable, not less.
entries.in_pinder: The tender message stands alone in its own message. The undercut follows in the next one, from the same or the other character, crude and specific in a way that confirms the feeling rather than denies it. Use it at the ending so the connection stays funny, and never put both in the same message.
entries.test: If you deleted the tender line, would the crude one still mean the same? If yes, it isn't exposing anything.
entries.goes_wrong: The undercut takes the feeling back ('jk'), which is a wink and a concession; or it comes so fast the tender line never gets its pause.

In the middle it works as a leak of the why. It also sets up the end: the reader waits to see whether the same plain feeling will ever be pointed at the match.

Put the detail in its own message and follow it with the act resuming or the other character going quiet. It is the brief's finding out why in compact form, best in the middle or at the reveal.

entries.name: A requested line that still lands
entries.summary: One character asks for an exact sentence, the other sends it, and it undoes the first one anyway.
entries.how_it_works: The reader expects a line someone was told to say to ring hollow. When it lands anyway, the laugh and the ache arrive together: it shows how badly the person needed to hear it, and that need is stronger than knowing it was scripted.
entries.in_pinder: One character asks the other to send a specific sentence, sometimes down to the capitalisation. The other sends it exactly, and the first is undone by it in a one-word reply. It belongs near the ending as a version of the short, plain tender line, and it is stronger if the requested words echo something set up earlier. Nobody comments on its being staged.

family.name: Holding a voice
family.about: Keeping a character straight-faced, specific and consistent in how they type and talk.

entries.name: The character must not know it's funny
entries.summary: Every message comes from someone who means it completely and whose attention is on their problem, never on being funny, so the reader is the one who notices.
entries.how_it_works: The laugh is the distance between what the speaker thinks is happening and what is. When the speaker shows they know a line is funny or strange, they have done the reader's noticing for them and the gap closes. When they are busy with something else, like workmen on an absurd statue worrying about the cement truck, the oddness is left on the screen for the reader to find, and finding it is the laugh.
entries.in_pinder: Each character believes their strategy is working and has a logic that holds from the inside; their attention is on getting the date, being understood or not being hurt. Write the strangest claims in ordinary punctuation, with no 'lol', 'haha', winking emoji or 'I know that sounds mad'. Message breaks are where awareness leaks in: a follow-up that apologises for the last line kills it, a follow-up that defends it doubles it. Self-deprecation is allowed only as a strategy the character believes in. If a character has a tell, it is tiny and involuntary, a dropped full stop or a reply too fast, never a comment.
entries.test: Delete every 'lol', 'haha', emoji, exclamation mark and line that points at the joke: if the message gets funnier, or breaks, it was relying on the wink. Then ask whether any message could be read as the character noticing they are failing or being funny; if so, cut it or turn it into a defence.
entries.goes_wrong: The character signals they're in on it ('ok that came out wrong haha', 'lol I'm such a mess'), calls themselves weird or adorable, reacts to their own punchline, or the writer mistakes unhinged for random so the inside logic no longer holds.

angles.author: Jenny Slate
angles.note: When the other is puzzled, the character answers with more sincere detail rather than laughing it off, and this matters most at the start and most of all for sweet characters, who must never know they are sweet.

angles.author: Steven Wright
angles.note: Keep the character's attention on the practical problem as they see it, so any giveaway is a small involuntary tell rather than a comment.

angles.author: Maria Bamford

entries.name: Deadpan that lives in the typing
entries.summary: After something catastrophic, the character types a calm, practical line that reacts far less than the event deserves.
entries.how_it_works: The disaster is large and the reaction is flat, and the gap between them is the laugh. Because the speaker never signals that anything is wrong, the reader has to supply the reaction, which makes them complicit in it.
entries.in_pinder: A reader can't see a blank face, so the flatness has to be on the screen: no exclamation marks, no 'haha', and the next message carries on as if the disaster were a small admin note. It is most useful straight after a mishap or a slip that gives the character away. Don't rely on a missing reply to carry it; the deadpan is a typed line, in this character's own typing style.
entries.test: Does the line react less than the event deserves, in this character's own typing style, with no sign they know it is odd?
entries.goes_wrong: Flatness that reads as cool irony puts the character above the joke, which is a wink; flat lines turn after turn kill the temperature changes the chat needs.

Use it once or twice at most; the next time, the character fails to dodge and sends the plainest line in the chat.

entries.name: Nickname as a defence
entries.summary: The character shrinks the match to a nickname, patches it each time the match doesn't fit, and at the end uses their real name.
entries.how_it_works: A nickname is a short, precise insult, so it lands as a joke on its own. Repeated, it shows the namer: someone who has to shrink people before they can deal with them. When the match doesn't fit the label, the nickname failing is the first sign the defence is failing.
entries.in_pinder: Let the character label the match, or people they mention, early and confidently, and reuse the label so it becomes a running bit. Each time the match does something off-label, the character amends the nickname rather than dropping it, so it gets longer and less accurate. The payoff is a late message that uses the match's actual name, plainly, with no label.
entries.test: Is the nickname specific enough to be funny on its own, and does the character ever have to patch it?
entries.goes_wrong: The labels are generic types ('fuckboy', 'nice guy') that say nothing about the namer, or the character explains that labelling keeps people at a distance.

entries.name: Quote the voice behind the habit

entries.name: Build the act against one specific fear
entries.summary: Name the one loss the character can't survive, then build the act so that they never have to feel it.
entries.how_it_works: Fleabag started from a question: what if she lost her best friend? The breezy, filthy act is built so she never has to feel that. Because the front is aimed at one specific fear, every joke points away from the same place, and the audience starts to feel the shape of what's missing. Her collaborator's wince was the check: if an idea made Vicky Jones wince, it went in.
entries.in_pinder: Before writing a character, name the specific loss they can't survive, and design the act as the thing that stops them feeling it. Every opener, brag and dodge in the chat should then point away from that loss, so the reader can work it out from what gets avoided. That answers the brief's end questions in advance: what are they afraid of, and what do they do so they don't have to feel it. This is planning work done before the first message. The character never says it.
entries.test: Can you name the specific loss, and does every one of the character's moves point away from it? If a joke points nowhere, cut it or redirect it.
entries.goes_wrong: The character announces the fear instead of avoiding it, or the fear is generic ('rejection') and the act has no shape.

Every message of the act should be that flaw producing a line. A register can carry the flaw, but keep the parody of it light; if it's obvious, the parody becomes the joke and the person disappears.

entries.goes_wrong: The character becomes a parody of a type with no fear behind it, and the reader can't say what they are afraid of.

entries.name: Fix the plan before the lines
entries.summary: Settle each character's fear, habit, origin and how the two habits collide before the first turn, because no line can make up for a missing one.
entries.how_it_works: A problem in the outline carries through to every later stage and finally reaches the audience. Jokes depend on what's underneath them: a surprise needs an expectation and a satisfying hit needs a setup, and both come from the story. Good lines on a weak structure get a laugh and leave nothing, because nobody is there to care about.
entries.in_pinder: Before the first turn, the plan states each character's fear, the habit that keeps them from feeling it, where the habit comes from, and how each habit lands on the other's sore spot. The setup items (an object, a phrase, a number) are fixed here, so the director can bring each one back once in the middle and the payoff can land without explanation. During the chat, the director checks each turn against the plan instead of chasing the best line.
entries.test: Before the chat starts, can you state for each character the fear, the habit, its origin, and how the two habits collide?
entries.goes_wrong: The why is left for the writer to find mid-chat, so the chat becomes good lines with no one underneath them; or the planned why turns up as a speech that explains it.

entries.name: Laugh at the defence, never the need
entries.summary: Every laugh lands on the act, the strategy or the dating-app belief, never on the loneliness, body or desire underneath.
entries.how_it_works: Fielder makes himself the fool and aims at systems and personas, so the audience can laugh freely: nobody is being punished for wanting something. When a joke lands on the need itself, the laugh turns into cruelty.
entries.in_pinder: Aim each laugh at the act, the bluff or the belief the app has taught the character, and keep the want underneath intact and visible. When a character is humiliated, it should be by their own strategy, not by the fact that they're lonely, horny or small. That is what lets the reader's laughter turn affectionate later instead of embarrassed.
entries.test: Is this joke laughing at what the character needs, or at how they defend themselves against needing it? If it's the need, rewrite it.
entries.goes_wrong: Punching at loneliness, a body or desire itself makes the chat cruel and the reader stops caring. Protecting the character so carefully that the act is never laughed at fails the other way.

entries.name: Ask why until it goes sad
entries.summary: Keep asking why the character does their thing until the answer is plain and old, then let one piece of it slip out in the middle.
entries.how_it_works: Seen once, a habit is a gag. Once the audience knows where it comes from, the same habit is sad, and laughing at it turns into affection. Robinson's writers found sketches with only one turn too slight, so they kept asking questions, like why he put the bumper sticker on in the first place, until one ended somewhere sincere.
entries.in_pinder: For each character's act, keep asking why until the answer is plain and old. In the middle, let one piece of it out in a single message, without explanation or reflection, then let the habit run again so it lands differently. Adjustment: many of Robinson's characters never get their why, but in Pinder every character must.
entries.test: After the reveal, does the next instance of the habit read differently, without anyone commenting on it?
entries.goes_wrong: The character explains the why in therapy language ('I think this comes from'), which does the reader's work for them; or the why never arrives and the habit stays a gag.

entries.name: No straight man: both are mad
entries.summary: Give both characters an act of their own, so the comedy comes from the two colliding rather than one sane person reacting to an oddball.
entries.how_it_works: When everyone is a little unhinged, nobody is singled out to be laughed at, and the comedy comes from the collision. That makes it warmer: Molly Fischer called it an 'expansive, even heartwarming' kind of cringe, and said it is why The Chair Company works where Friendship, with one oddball among straight men, didn't.
entries.in_pinder: Neither character spends the whole chat as the sane one reacting. Whoever reacts in one stretch should have their own act for the other to react to in the next. Plan the two acts so they collide, especially in the middle.
entries.test: Over the whole chat, has each character been the one in trouble at least once?
entries.goes_wrong: One character deadpans all the way through and becomes the reader's stand-in, so the other one feels mocked rather than loved.

entries.name: Write the other side of the chat properly
entries.summary: The character answering a scheme needs their own logic and fear on every turn; a plain, believable reply is what shows how strange the scheme is.
entries.how_it_works: Fielder's schemes are funny because a real person answers them normally, and that ordinary reply is what measures how strange the scheme is. His comedy borrows that half from real people. Written reactions have to supply it, and when they aren't believable the discomfort goes flat, as critics said of the invented side characters in The Curse.
entries.in_pinder: Write the other character's replies as specific, plausible answers that come from their own act and fear, not as feed lines. A plain, honest question or an ordinary fact often does more than a comeback, because it shows the first character's plan for what it is. Both sides need a logic of their own on every turn.
entries.test: Cover one character's lines. Does the other still read as a person with their own reasons, or only as a prompt?
entries.goes_wrong: The reacting character becomes a prop who only says 'what' and 'lol ok', so the scheme has nothing to land against and the reader never learns what the second person is afraid of.

entries.name: The partner who asks the next question
entries.summary: Put the rising disbelief into the other character's short, plain questions, each one pulling a worse detail out of the one who is doubling down.
entries.how_it_works: Rising disbelief tells the audience that each new fact is worse than the last, and they enjoy the pile-up. In stand-up the comedian supplies the reaction himself.
entries.in_pinder: Adjustment: no character can narrate their disbelief, so it goes into the other character's short replies, each a plain question asking for the next detail ('how many', 'labelled how'). Each short reply against a longer message works as a reaction shot, and each question pulls a worse answer out of the character who won't back down. It belongs in the middle, beside a character who is doubling down.
entries.test: Is every reply from the questioner shorter than the message it answers, and does it ask rather than judge?
entries.goes_wrong: The questioner editorialises ('wow ok that's insane') and becomes a commentator, or asks so many questions that they have no act of their own.

entries.name: Never explain the joke after it lands
entries.summary: End on the punchline; any explanation next to it does the reader's work and kills the laugh.
entries.how_it_works: A joke works because the reader closes the gap themselves; an explanation closes it for them and takes the click away. Explaining also shows the speaker doubts the joke, which amounts to a wink. Context that comes much later can deepen a joke, but context right next to it kills it.
entries.in_pinder: End the run of messages on the punchline. If the other character needs to react, give them one word or a question, not a recap. Save any background that would explain the line for much later, where it changes the meaning instead of explaining it. Watch especially for a character's own follow-up message that starts with 'like' or 'because' after a strong line.
entries.test: Cover the message after the punchline. If the chat is just as clear and funnier without it, delete it.
entries.goes_wrong: A character adds 'because I'm insecure about my size' after a size joke, or the other character explains a callback back to them.

entries.name: Stop when the logic is complete
entries.summary: End a run, and the chat, on the message that completes it, with nothing after it that softens or recaps.
entries.how_it_works: Cutting the moment the last piece falls into place leaves the audience holding the whole picture without anyone explaining it. Every line after that point lets the air out. Robinson's sketches end abruptly as soon as the logic is complete, and his writers cut heavily because too much of it in a row is exhausting.
entries.in_pinder: When a run reaches its worst or truest line, end the run there: no softening message, no recap, no 'anyway'. The same goes for the chat's last message, which is often the shortest one and completes the logic. Adjustment: a sketch can cut off mid-shout, but a Pinder ending still has to make the connection or the collapse readable.
entries.test: Is the last message of the run the one that completes it, with nothing after it that explains or softens it?
entries.goes_wrong: An extra 'haha anyway' after the line that landed; or cutting so early that the reader can't yet say what each of them was afraid of.

entries.name: Surprise them or satisfy them
entries.summary: Decide whether each beat surprises the reader or gives them the hit they saw coming; the collapse should be the second kind.
entries.how_it_works: Surprise is the turn nobody saw coming. Satisfaction is the audience predicting the hit and getting exactly that, which feels like being proved right. Knowing the plot in advance kills both, so a satisfying hit has to be foreseeable from the setup but never announced.
entries.in_pinder: Decide which kind each beat is. Early jokes about the act are mostly surprise; the collapse should be satisfaction, where the reader has watched a habit all chat and it lands exactly on the other one's sore spot. For satisfaction, the danger must be visible at least a turn early; for surprise, nothing in the previous message should point at it.
entries.test: Can you say which kind this beat is? If it's satisfaction, is its setup on the screen at least a turn earlier?
entries.goes_wrong: A satisfaction beat with no visible setup lands as random, and a surprise that the other character predicts out loud ('bet you're going to say...') is neither.

origins.text: Clement says a joke either surprises people or delivers what they expect and satisfies them; the report says the second kind fits Pinder's inevitable ending.

entries.name: Say it aloud before it's sent
entries.summary: Draft each message as this character would actually type it mid-conversation, and cut anything that sounds clever or saved up.
entries.how_it_works: Horgan and Delaney say their lines aloud, transcribe them and read them aloud again, so nobody sounds clever or written. Spoken speech is halting, specific and slightly wrong; written dialogue is balanced and pleased with itself. Lines that come out of a mouth carry the speaker's tics and evasions, and that's where character and laughs live. Polish gives the writer away, and once the audience senses the writer they stop believing the person.
entries.in_pinder: Draft each message by saying it the way this particular dick would at one in the morning, then type it with their capitalisation, punctuation and typos. Cut balanced phrasing, wordplay the character couldn't have found under pressure, and any line that sounds saved up. Horgan's characters are openly sharp, but Pinder's characters think they're being sensible: take the honesty, not the wit.
entries.test: Would a real person type this, unedited, in the middle of a conversation, or does it sound saved up?
entries.goes_wrong: The quip: a neat line that fills a turn, shows off the writer and gives nothing away about the character.

origins.author: Sharon Horgan
origins.text: Horgan and Delaney's rule is to try not to have anybody sound clever or written: they say lines aloud, transcribe them and read them aloud again, and the report calls this the most useful process rule, equivalent to Pinder's ban on characters who know they're funny.

entries.name: Name the territory, find the line live
entries.summary: The director gives the subject and the pressure, not the punchline; the writer builds the line from the exact words of the message before.
entries.how_it_works: Improvised lines lose their life when they are written into the script, so the subject is left open and the performer finds the line. A line found in the moment answers what just happened, so it sounds like the character rather than a prepared joke. A pre-written line comes out stiff because it can't react to the words it follows.
entries.in_pinder: The director names the territory and the pressure ('she mentions her ex; he takes the ex's insult as a compliment and runs with it'), not the punchline. The writer builds the line from what is actually on the screen, ideally picking up a specific word from the previous message and bending it. That keeps the chat responsive and keeps each character's act running into the other's actual words.
entries.test: Does the director's note name a territory and a pressure rather than a line, and does the written line pick up something specific from the message before it?
entries.goes_wrong: The director writes the punchline and it gets pasted in even though the last message has moved somewhere else; or the territory is so vague it gives the writer nothing to work with.
